idiom_name: static AtomicBool flag + explicit load_flags at start-up
implementation_notes: The runtime realization is a standard-library primitive rather than a framework: a static AtomicBool (lock-free on every supported target) is the flag state, an explicit load_flags call at start-up parses the environment or configuration once, and the toggle point is a load(Ordering::Relaxed) followed by a branch. Relaxed is sufficient when the flag only selects a path; a flag that guards lazily built data needs release/acquire, and a whole parsed configuration struct that must be created on first use belongs behind OnceLock (Rust 1.70) or a Mutex rather than in a bare static. Reach for a trait-object decision (or a provider crate such as an OpenFeature SDK) when flags need targeting or an audit trail, and use the Cargo-feature variant when the code must not be compiled at all.
pitfalls: Ordering::Relaxed is enough to publish a choice, not to publish data: use Release/Acquire (or OnceLock) when the flag gates initialisation, or another thread can observe the flag as on before the data exists.
A `static mut` would compile but is unsound; interior mutability (AtomicBool, OnceLock, Mutex) is the only way a static can change at runtime.
cfg!(feature = "...") looks like a runtime check but is resolved at compile time, so using it where a runtime switch was promised quietly reintroduces a rebuild.

variants.name: Cargo features via #[cfg(feature = "...")]
variants.implementation_notes: Rust's native build-time mechanism: features declared in the [features] table of Cargo.toml are set by the build system with --cfg, and #[cfg(feature = "new-checkout")] (or the cfg! macro for a boolean) selects code or optional dependencies at compile time. Disabled code is not compiled at all, so it costs nothing at runtime and cannot be flipped in production without a rebuild - which is precisely why this is a variant and not the pattern's default realization: it is the build-time binding of the same decision, useful for optional integrations and platform or backend variants.
pitfalls: Feature unification: enabling a feature anywhere in the dependency graph enables it for every crate in the build, so an unrelated dependency can switch your flag on.
Each feature combination is a separate compilation; CI that builds only default features never compiles the gated path, so it rots until release day.
